title: Vasectomies: Stop Being A Wimp
summary: Josh and Chuck explain vasectomy: what the procedure is, why it is simpler, cheaper and faster to recover from than tubal ligation, and why men are less likely to get one. They cover the vas deferens, semen versus sperm, the no-scalpel method, post-op precautions, the roughly 15 to 20 ejaculations needed to clear sperm and the follow-up sperm test, risks and chronic pain, sexual function myths, reversal and its success rates, and emerging reversible gel methods. The episode closes with the history of vasectomy in eugenics (Harry Sharp, Albert Osterhout, forced sterilizations, Switzerland's Roma), Eugen Steinach's discredited vasectomy-for-virility idea, a March Madness vasectomy factoid, and a listener mail about Sources of Strength suicide prevention.

segments.title: Opening and vasectomy basics
segments.summary: The hosts introduce vasectomy as a simple, quick, low-cost procedure with fast recovery, compare it with tubal ligation, and note that it prevents pregnancy but not STIs. They discuss male-female sterilization disparities and common myths about vasectomy.

segments.title: Effectiveness, cost, and recovery compared
segments.summary: Vasectomy is nearly 100 percent effective, compared with the pullout method (about 78 percent) and condoms (about 85 percent). Cost is about $1,000 versus roughly six times that for tubal ligation, which requires general anesthesia and a longer recovery. Insurance coverage differences in the US are noted.

segments.title: Sperm, semen, and the vas deferens
segments.summary: The hosts explain that semen is fluid and sperm is only a component, and that the vas deferens carries sperm from the testes and mixes it with seminal fluids. A vasectomy cuts the vas deferens so sperm is removed from semen. The name comes from the vas deferens.

segments.title: The procedure and no-scalpel method
segments.summary: The procedure is done under local anesthesia in about 20 minutes or less. The surgeon makes small incisions in the scrotum, pulls out each vas deferens, cuts it, and seals it by stitching, cauterizing, or both. A no-scalpel method uses a punch tool to make a small puncture instead of an incision. An open-end vasectomy leaves the tube open so sperm is absorbed in the scrotum.

segments.title: Recovery, sperm absorption, and clearing the system
segments.summary: Sperm is absorbed by the body in the epididymis rather than building up. Recovery involves rest for about 24 to 48 hours, supportive underwear, cold packs, and pain relievers, with about a week before sports or sex. Around 15 to 20 ejaculations are needed to clear sperm, and a sperm test about six to twelve weeks later confirms success.

segments.title: Risks, sexual function, and testosterone
segments.summary: Risks include infection, blood clots, blood in semen, and bruising, which usually clear up. Chronic pain affects one to two percent, and a spermatocele can develop. Vasectomy does not affect testosterone, erection, orgasm, or sex drive, and a German study reported greater sexual satisfaction.

segments.title: Reversal, reconalization, and reversible methods
segments.summary: About six percent of men seek reversal, which costs $5,000 to $15,000 and has variable success. IVF with sperm retrieval is an alternative. Reconalization causes the vas deferens to regrow. Researchers are developing reversible gel-based blockages, and male pill safety testing is discussed.

segments.title: History: eugenics and forced sterilization
segments.summary: Vasectomy was used for eugenics starting in the mid-1800s with veterinary experiments on dogs. Harry Sharp performed a nonmedical vasectomy on a teenage inmate in Indiana. Albert Osterhout advocated sterilizing criminals. About 320,000 forced sterilizations occurred through World War Two, and Switzerland targeted the Roma until 1972. The Nazis also sterilized people.

segments.title: Steinach's discredited virility procedure and March Madness
segments.summary: Eugen Steinach believed cutting one vas deferens would boost testosterone; figures like Sigmund Freud and William Yeats tried it, but the claim was discredited. A trivia item states vasectomies rose about 30 percent during the first round of NCAA basketball tournament time, which is noted as correlation not necessarily causation.

segments.title: Listener mail: Sources of Strength
segments.summary: Listener Mark Counts writes about the Sources of Strength youth-led suicide prevention program, used in schools in the US, Canada, and Australia, and his work with Clark County schools in Ohio during Suicide Prevention Month. The hosts thank him.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and remind listeners how to send mail.
